item.title: Child malnutrition: 150.2 million under-5s are stunted. In Africa, the number is still rising.
item.description:
Dev Data Weekly #04

Key takeaways

  1. 150.2 million children under 5 worldwide were stunted in 2024 (too short for their age, a sign of long-term undernutrition). That is 23.2% of young children, down from 26.4% in 2012.
  2. Africa is the only region where the number of stunted children under 5 has grown: from 61.7 million in 2012 to 64.8 million in 2024. Asia and Africa together are home to 94% of stunted young children.
  3. About 412 million children lived on less than US$3 a day in 2024 (World Bank and UNICEF). Separately, UNICEF counts 417 million children in low- and middle-income countries severely deprived in at least two basics, such as nutrition or sanitation.

item.title: Extreme weather killed 832,000 people in 30 years. 6 of the 10 hardest-hit countries are lower-middle-income.
item.description:
Dev Data Weekly #03

Key takeaways

  1. Extreme weather (storms, floods, heat waves and more) killed more than 832,000 people worldwide in 1995–2024 and caused over US$4.5 trillion in direct losses, according to the Germanwatch Climate Risk Index.
  2. Of the 10 countries hit hardest by extreme weather in 1995–2024, 6 are lower-middle-income. Dominica, Myanmar and Honduras top the list.
  3. In rural areas of 24 low- and middle-income countries, households headed by women lose 8% more of their income to heat stress and 3% more to floods each year than households headed by men (FAO).

item.title: Rich countries delivered $136.7 billion in climate finance. The poorest got 7%.
item.description:
Dev Data Weekly #02

Key takeaways

  1. Rich countries gave or mobilised US$136.7 billion in climate finance for developing countries in 2024. To meet the new goal of US$300 billion a year by 2035, that must grow about 2.2×.
  2. The poorest (low-income) countries received just 7% of that climate finance in 2024.
  3. To adapt to climate change (for example flood defences or drought-resistant farming), developing countries will need US$310–365 billion a year by 2035. In 2023 they received US$26 billion in international public funding for this.

item.title: 239 million people need humanitarian aid. The plan targets 87 million.
item.description:
Dev Data Weekly #01

Key takeaways

  1. 239 million people need humanitarian aid in 2026. With less money available, the UN plan focuses first on 87 million of them (36%).
  2. Helping those 87 million people requires US$23 billion. Separately, aid reached 25 million fewer people in 2025 than in 2024.
  3. The donor mix is shifting: the United States went from about 40% of government humanitarian funding (before 2025) to 23% in 2025, while Gulf donors rose from 10% to 17%.
